The '''Taft equation''' is a [[Free-energy relationship|linear free energy relationship]] (LFER) used in [[physical organic chemistry]] in the study of [[reaction mechanism]]s and in  the development of [[quantitative structure–activity relationship]]s for [[organic compound]]s.  It was developed by [[Robert W. Taft]] in 1952<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Taft|first=Robert W.|date=June 1952|title=Linear Free Energy Relationships from Rates of Esterification and Hydrolysis of Aliphatic and Ortho-substituted Benzoate Esters|url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/ja01131a010|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|language=en|volume=74|issue=11|pages=2729–2732|doi=10.1021/ja01131a010|issn=0002-7863|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Taft|first=Robert W.|date=1952-06-01|title=Polar and Steric Substituent Constants for Aliphatic and o-Benzoate Groups from Rates of Esterification and Hydrolysis of Esters1|url=https://doi.org/10.1021/ja01132a049|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|volume=74|issue=12|pages=3120–3128|doi=10.1021/ja01132a049|issn=0002-7863|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Taft|first=Robert W.|date=1953-09-01|title=Linear Steric Energy Relationships|url=https://doi.org/10.1021/ja01114a044|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|volume=75|issue=18|pages=4538–4539|doi=10.1021/ja01114a044|issn=0002-7863|url-access=subscription}}</ref> as a modification to the [[Hammett equation]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Hammett|first=Louis P.|date=1937-01-01|title=The Effect of Structure upon the Reactions of Organic Compounds. Benzene Derivatives|url=https://doi.org/10.1021/ja01280a022|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|volume=59|issue=1|pages=96–103|doi=10.1021/ja01280a022|issn=0002-7863|url-access=subscription}}</ref>  While the Hammett equation accounts for how [[substituent field effect|field]], [[Inductive effect|inductive]], and [[Mesomeric effect|resonance]] effects influence reaction rates, the Taft equation also describes the [[steric effects]] of a [[substituent]].  The Taft equation is written as:

:<math chem>\log\left ( \frac{k_s}{k_{\ce{CH3}}} \right )= \rho^*\sigma^* + \delta E_s</math>

where <math chem>\log\frac{k_s}{k_\ce{CH3}}</math> is the ratio of the [[reaction rate|rate]] of the substituted reaction compared to the reference reaction, ρ* is the sensitivity factor for the reaction to [[polar effect]]s, σ* is the polar substituent constant that describes the field and inductive effects of the substituent, δ is the sensitivity factor for the reaction to steric effects, and E<sub>s</sub> is the steric substituent constant.

== Polar substituent constants, σ*==

Polar substituent constants describe the way a substituent will influence a reaction through polar (inductive, field, and resonance) effects.  To determine σ<sup>*</sup> Taft studied the [[hydrolysis]] of [[methyl]] [[esters]] (RCOOMe).  The use of ester hydrolysis rates to study polar effects was first suggested by Ingold in 1930.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Ainley|first1=Arthur Donald|last2=Challenger|first2=Frederick|date=1930-01-01|title=CCLXXX.—Studies of the boron–carbon linkage. Part I. The oxidation and nitration of phenylboric acid|url=https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlelanding/1930/jr/jr9300002171|journal=Journal of the Chemical Society (Resumed)|language=en|pages=2171–2180|doi=10.1039/JR9300002171|issn=0368-1769|url-access=subscription}}</ref>  The hydrolysis of esters can occur through either [[acid catalysis|acid and base catalyzed mechanisms]], both of which proceed through a [[Tetrahedral molecular geometry|tetrahedral]] [[reactive intermediate|intermediate]].  In the base catalyzed mechanism the reactant goes from a neutral species to negatively charged intermediate in the [[rate-determining step|rate determining (slow) step]], while in the acid catalyzed mechanism a positively charged reactant goes to a positively charged intermediate.

:[[Image:Wikipedia ester hydrolysis.png]]

Due to the similar tetrahedral intermediates, Taft proposed that under identical conditions any steric factors should be nearly the same for the two mechanisms and therefore would not influence the ratio of the rates.  However, because of the difference in charge buildup in the rate determining steps it was proposed that polar effects would only influence the reaction rate of the base catalyzed reaction since a new charge was formed.  He defined the polar substituent constant σ* as:

:<math chem>\sigma^* = \left( \frac{1}{2.48\rho^*} \right )\Bigg[\log\left( \frac{k_s}{k_{\ce{CH3}}} \right )_B - \log\left( \frac{k_s}{k_{\ce{CH3}}} \right )_A \Bigg]</math>

where log(k<sub>s</sub>/k<sub>CH<sub>3</sub></sub>)<sub>B</sub> is the ratio of the rate of the base catalyzed reaction compared to the reference reaction, log(k<sub>s</sub>/k<sub>CH<sub>3</sub></sub>)<sub>A</sub> is ratio of a rate of the acid catalyzed reaction compared to the reference reaction, and ρ* is a reaction constant that describes the sensitivity of the reaction series.  For the definition reaction series, ρ* was set to 1 and R = methyl was defined as the reference reaction (σ* = zero).  The factor of 1/2.48 is included to make σ* similar in magnitude to the [[Hammett equation#Substituent constants|Hammett σ values]].

== Steric substituent constants, E<sub>s</sub>==

Although the acid catalyzed and base catalyzed hydrolysis of esters gives [[transition state]]s for the rate determining steps that have differing [[charge density|charge densities]], their structures differ only by two [[hydrogen]] atoms.  Taft thus assumed that steric effects would influence both reaction mechanisms equally.  Due to this, the steric substituent constant E<sub>s</sub> was determined from solely the acid catalyzed reaction, as this would not include polar effects.  E<sub>s</sub> was defined as:

:<math chem>E_s = \frac {1}{\delta}\log\left ( \frac{k_s}{k_{\ce{CH3}}} \right )</math>

where ''k<sub>s</sub>'' is the rate of the studied reaction and <chem>\mathit k_{CH3}</chem> is the rate of the reference reaction (R = methyl).  δ is a reaction constant that describes the susceptibility of a reaction series to steric effects.  For the definition reaction series δ was set to 1 and ''E<sub>s</sub>'' for the reference reaction was set to zero.  This equation is combined with the equation for σ* to give the full Taft equation.

From comparing the ''E<sub>s</sub>'' values for methyl, [[ethyl group|ethyl]], [[isopropyl]], and [[tert-butyl]], it is seen that the value increases with increasing steric bulk.  However, because context will have an effect on steric interactions<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=McClelland|first1=Robert A.|last2=Steenken|first2=Steen.|date=1988-08-01|title=Radiation chemical production, lifetimes, and structure-activity relations for .alpha.-dialkoxyalkyl carbocations in aqueous solutions: Importance of solvation for cation reactivity|url=https://doi.org/10.1021/ja00225a042|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|volume=110|issue=17|pages=5860–5866|doi=10.1021/ja00225a042|issn=0002-7863|url-access=subscription}}</ref> some ''E<sub>s</sub>'' values can be larger or smaller than expected.  For example, the value for [[phenyl group|phenyl]] is much larger than that for ''tert''-butyl.  When comparing these groups using another measure of steric bulk, [[A value|axial strain values]], the ''tert''-butyl group is larger.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Anslyn, Eric V., 1960-|title=Modern physical organic chemistry|date=2006|publisher=University Science Books|others=Dougherty, Dennis A., 1952-|isbn=1-891389-31-9|location=Mill Valley, California|oclc=55600610}}</ref>

=== Other steric parameters for LFERs===

In addition to Taft's steric parameter ''E<sub>s</sub>'', other steric parameters that are independent of kinetic data have been defined.  Charton has defined values ''v''  that are derived from [[van der Waals radius|van der Waals radii]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Charton|first=Marvin|date=1975-03-01|title=Steric effects. I. Esterification and acid-catalyzed hydrolysis of esters|url=https://doi.org/10.1021/ja00839a047|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|volume=97|issue=6|pages=1552–1556|doi=10.1021/ja00839a047|issn=0002-7863|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Charton|first=Marvin.|date=1976-06-01|title=Steric effects. 7. Additional V constants|url=https://doi.org/10.1021/jo00874a035|journal=The Journal of Organic Chemistry|volume=41|issue=12|pages=2217–2220|doi=10.1021/jo00874a035|issn=0022-3263|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Using [[molecular mechanics]], Meyers has defined ''V''<sup>a</sup> values that are derived from the volume of the portion of the substituent that is within 0.3&nbsp;nm of the reaction center.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Meyer|first=Amatzya Y.|date=1986-01-01|title=Molecular mechanics and molecular shape. Part 4. Size, shape, and steric parameters|url=https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlelanding/1986/p2/p29860001567|journal=Journal of the Chemical Society, Perkin Transactions 2|language=en|issue=10|pages=1567–1572|doi=10.1039/P29860001567|issn=1364-5471|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

==Sensitivity factors==
===Polar sensitivity factor, ρ*===
Similar to [[Hammett equation#Rho value|ρ values]] for Hammett plots, the polar sensitivity factor ρ* for Taft plots will describe the susceptibility of a reaction series to polar effects.  When the steric effects of substituents do not significantly influence the reaction rate the Taft equation simplifies to a form of the Hammett equation:

:<math chem>\log \left (\frac {k_s}{k_{\ce{CH3}}}\right ) = \rho^*\sigma^*</math>

The polar sensitivity factor ρ* can be obtained by plotting the ratio of the measured reaction rates (''k<sub>s</sub>'') compared to the reference reaction (<chem>\mathit k_{CH3}</chem>) versus the σ* values for the substituents.  This plot will give a straight line with a [[slope]] equal to ρ*.  Similar to the Hammett ρ value:

* If ρ* > 1, the reaction accumulates negative charge in the transition state and is accelerated by [[Polar effect|electron withdrawing groups]].
* If 1 > ρ* > 0, negative charge is built up and the reaction is mildly sensitive to polar effects.
* If ρ* = 0, the reaction is not influenced by polar effects.
* If 0 > ρ* > −1, positive charge is built up and the reaction is mildly sensitive to polar effects.
* If −1 > ρ*, the reaction accumulates positive charge and is accelerated by [[polar effect|electron donating groups]].

===Steric sensitivity factor, δ===

Similar to the polar sensitivity factor, the steric sensitivity factor δ for a new reaction series will describe to what magnitude the reaction rate is influenced by steric effects.  When a reaction series is not significantly influenced by polar effects, the Taft equation reduces to:

:<math chem>\log \left (\frac {k_s}{k_{\ce{CH3}}}\right ) = \delta E_s</math>

A plot of the ratio of the rates versus the ''E<sub>s</sub>'' value for the substituent will give a straight line with a slope equal to δ.  Similarly to the Hammett ρ value, the magnitude of δ will reflect to what extent a reaction is influenced by steric effects:

*A very steep slope will correspond to high steric sensitivity, while a shallow slope will correspond to little to no sensitivity.
Since ''E<sub>s</sub>'' values are large and ''negative'' for bulkier substituents, it follows that:
*If δ is positive, increasing steric bulk decreases the reaction rate and steric effects are greater in the transition state.
*If δ is negative, increasing steric bulk increases the reaction rate and steric effects are lessened in the transition state.

===Reactions influenced by polar and steric effects===

When both steric and polar effects influence the reaction rate the Taft equation can be solved for both ρ* and δ through the use of standard [[least squares]] methods for determining a [[bivariant regression plane]].  Taft outlined the application of this method to solving the Taft equation in a 1957 paper.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Pavelich|first1=William A.|last2=Taft|first2=Robert W.|date=1957-09-01|title=The Evaluation of Inductive and Steric Effects on Reactivity. The Methoxide Ioncatalyzed Rates of Methanolysis of l-Menthyl Esters in Methanol1|url=https://doi.org/10.1021/ja01575a029|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|volume=79|issue=18|pages=4935–4940|doi=10.1021/ja01575a029|issn=0002-7863|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

==Taft plots in QSAR==

The Taft equation is often employed in [[biochemistry|biological chemistry]] and [[medicinal chemistry]] for the development of [[quantitative structure–activity relationship]]s (QSARs).  In a recent example, Sandri and co-workers<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Arcelli|first1=Antonio|last2=Porzi|first2=Gianni|last3=Rinaldi|first3=Samuele|last4=Sandri|first4=Monica|date=2008|title=Electrostatic interactions effect in the aminolysis of some β-lactams in the presence of poly(ethyleneimine):structure-reactivity|url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/poc.1301|journal=Journal of Physical Organic Chemistry|language=en|volume=21|issue=2|pages=163–172|doi=10.1002/poc.1301|issn=1099-1395|url-access=subscription}}</ref> have used Taft plots in studies of polar effects in the [[aminolysis]] of [[Beta-lactam|β-lactams]].  They have looked at the binding of β-lactams to a poly(ethyleneimine) [[polymer]], which functions as a simple mimic for [[human serum albumin]] (HSA).  The formation of a [[covalent bond]] between penicillins and HSA as a result of aminolysis with [[lysine]] residues is believed to be involved in [[Penicillin#Side effects|penicillin allergies]].  As a part of their mechanistic studies Sandri and co-workers plotted the rate of aminolysis versus calculated σ* values for 6 penicillins and found no correlation, suggesting that the rate is influenced by other effects in addition to polar and steric effects.
